title: Two AIs Agreeing Doesn’t Make Them Right
body_markdown:
*By Jason Vantomme and Peter Hogan, Workday AI Platform*


If you build agents for HR and finance, you’ve probably seen this one: A manager asks whether they can approve an exception to a spending limit. The agent returns a confident answer, a clean explanation, and a citation to the right policy. Everything looks correct. But look closer, and the policy never settles the question. A person was supposed to decide, and the agent filled the gap with something that sounded authoritative.


The usual fix is intuitive: add a second model to review the first model’s work. We tested that fix in the research behind our upcoming paper. It doesn’t work the way you’d hope.


### TL;DR:


- **Plausible but unsupported inference** is a failure where an agent has the right source and still produces an answer the source does not support.
- In our tests, models recognized genuine uncertainty in only 25% of the cases where it was present.
- Whether a second model helped depended on which one did the checking: one judge improved accuracy by about 4 points, one lowered it by about 4, and one made no detectable difference.
- Judge models made their worst mistakes on exactly the questions that need a second opinion most.
- Two models agreeing tells you an answer is plausible. It does not tell you the answer follows from the source.


### The Failure That Looks Like Success


Most conversations about AI errors center on models inventing facts. Retrieval helps there, because it puts the right documents in front of the model.


In this failure, the agent already has the correct source and may read every clause correctly. What breaks is the step from source to answer. The model treats a policy as if it resolves a question when it does not, or it skips a provision that would change the result. Having the right evidence in front of the model does not guarantee the answer is supported by it, and a citation can be accurate while the claim attached to it is still wrong \[1\].


We call this **plausible but unsupported inference** . It matters in enterprise settings because it looks exactly like a correct answer. There is no typo to catch and no obvious fabrication.


### What We Tested


For this research, we built a synthetic policy corpus around a year-end sales incentive true-up, covering five representative populations, and wrote 118 questions against it. Some had clear answers. Others were built so the source contradicts itself or deliberately leaves the decision to case-by-case human judgment, which means the correct response is to escalate to a person instead of answering.


We compared two setups:


1. **Baseline:** a foundation model answers directly from the source documents with no verification step.
2. **LLM-as-judge:** a second model, the judge, reviews the first model’s answer against the same evidence. The judge always came from a different, independently developed model family than the model it was checking, so no model ever checked its own work.


We ran six models across three independent families. Each model’s answers were reviewed by the judge models from the other two families.


### Finding 1: Confidence Wins Over Recognition


On questions with a clear answer, the models did well, with accuracy of 88% to 90%.


On questions where the right move was to recognize genuine uncertainty, they struggled. Pooled across all six models, they recognized the uncertainty in only 25% of those cases. The rest of the time, they answered confidently anyway. Other researchers have found that, on general-purpose benchmarks, models struggle to admit when a question can’t be answered \[2\]. We saw the same pattern in an enterprise policy setting, even though the models had the complete policy in front of them.


In one case, a model’s own written explanation said the steps of a required process were “explicitly not defined” in the source. It then returned a confident, multi-step procedure anyway. Its awareness of the gap did not change its answer. In another, two models went further and built a coherent justification for a calculation rule the source never states. That is harder to catch than silence, because the response reads like careful reasoning.


The confusion also ran the other way: when models did escalate, they were wrong more than half the time. They could not reliably tell when to be confident and when to hand off.


### Finding 2: A Second Model Helps Unevenly


Adding a judge model did not move accuracy in a single direction. The effect depended on which model did the checking. One judge improved accuracy by about 4 percentage points, one lowered it by about 4, and one made no detectable difference.


Judge models also caused damage, and it landed on the questions that matter most. When a baseline model correctly escalated a question to a person, the judge overturned that correct answer at approximately 3.9 times the rate it did on any other kind of question. And when a baseline model wrongly answered a question that should have been escalated, judge models endorsed the wrong answer 73% of the time, compared with 41% on other kinds of questions. These comparisons rest on a small number of questions, so treat them as a pattern, not a precise rate.


### Finding 3: A Judge Model Can Contradict Itself


In one case, a judge model examined a correct answer and wrote that it was “fully justified by the source materials” and “appropriate in substance.” Then it marked the answer incorrect anyway, citing only a labeling technicality.


In another case, the policy documents said the system must not give a binary answer to a certain type of question. One model opened with “Yes,” added that the matter “requires a case-by-case determination,” yet still delivered the whole thing as a direct answer. The judge model called that answer “correct and precisely grounded.” Both models treated it as a question with a clear answer, which is exactly what the policy said it wasn’t.


Part of the problem traced to a single weak judge model, which overturned correct answers far more often than the other two. Removing it would eliminate most of that effect. But the self-contradiction in the first example came from a judge model that was otherwise reliable, which points to a limit of the approach itself and not just one bad judge \[3\].


### Why Agreement Isn’t Proof


Imagine you ask two colleagues whether the travel policy covers a particular expense. Both say yes, and both sound sure. That doesn’t settle it. Two colleagues agreeing tells you what they both believe. It doesn’t tell you what the policy says. Agreement tells you about the people in the room. Only the policy tells you about the policy.


A second model reviewing the first works the same way. Our judge models were never from the same family as the model they were checking, and the failure still recurred \[4\]. That suggests the problem is not simply a model missing its own blind spots. Agreement is a signal that an answer is plausible. It is not a check that the answer is supported.


Other published research on formalizing natural-language policy into logic and checking it with a solver points in the same direction: reliable checking needs independent, redundant steps and not a single generative pass \[5\]. What is missing is a mechanism that can establish, consistently and regardless of which models are involved, that an answer is supported by its source. A second model can serve as a useful extra signal. It cannot be that mechanism.


### What This Means for Builders


1. **Test for the gap, not just the answer.** Build evaluation sets where the correct response is “the source does not resolve this.” Accuracy on answerable questions tells you little about this behavior, and the two can diverge sharply.
2. **Do not treat a judge model’s approval as verification.** A second model catches some errors and introduces others. Measure it on your own data, by question type and by which model does the judging, before it becomes a control you rely on.
3. **Check the answer against the source, not just the source’s availability.** Retrieval and citations get evidence in front of the model. Plan separately for how you will confirm the answer is actually supported by that evidence.
4. **Treat escalation as a first-class outcome.** In HR and finance workflows, a well-routed handoff to a person is a correct answer, but only if the system can tell when a handoff is needed. Systems should be scored, and designed, accordingly.


### Where This Leaves Us


Agents are taking on work where a confident wrong answer has real consequences for employees, customers, and the companies responsible for them. In that setting, “sounds right and cites a source” is not a sufficient bar, and neither is “a second model agreed.” The standard worth building toward is an answer that can be shown to follow from the governing source, with a clear handoff to a person when it cannot.


Our tests used a single-domain synthetic corpus, a small set of genuine-uncertainty questions, and single-turn queries only, so we read these results as a strong signal and not a final measurement. That leaves open questions worth exploring. One is whether the confidence we observed reflects a failure to see the gap or a reluctance to act on it. Another is whether letting an agent ask a clarifying question changes the outcome. Larger and more varied policy corpora would also show how far the pattern extends, and a same-family review comparison would show how much of the problem is a shared blind spot. What we can say today is that it held across every independently developed model family we tried, which tells us this isn’t one provider’s problem. Our upcoming paper details the full method, results, and case analyses.


### References


1. [RAGTruth: A Hallucination Corpus for Retrieval-Augmented Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00396)
2. [AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038)
3. [The Stability Trap: Evaluating the Reliability of LLM-Based Instruction Adherence Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11783)
4. [Correlated Errors in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962)
5. [A Neurosymbolic Approach to Natural Language Formalization and Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09008)
